abstract: Understanding the economic impacts of drought remains challenging, particularly in identifying causal effects and accounting for regional heterogeneity. This paper applies the Synthetic Control Method (SCM) to estimate the impact of the 2017–2020 drought on economic returns to agricultural labour across three main agricultural regions in New South Wales, Australia. Using a 30‐year panel from the ABARES Australian Agricultural and Grazing Industries Survey, we construct counterfactual trajectories for total cash receipts per unit of labour to assess how outcomes would have evolved in the absence of drought. The results reveal substantial spatial heterogeneity in both the magnitude and persistence of impacts: the North West region experienced a decline of approximately 57% but recovered by 2022, the Central West shows persistent losses relative to its counterfactual by 2022, and the Riverina exhibits only limited deviations, suggesting greater resilience. These findings highlight that drought impacts differ not only in severity but also in recovery dynamics across regions and demonstrate the value of SCM as a transparent and replicable approach for estimating regional economic impacts using publicly available data, with important implications for place‐based drought policy.
title: Drought Impacts and Recovery Across Agricultural Regions: Evidence on Farm Economic Returns to Labour From a Synthetic Control Analysis

abstract: Amid overlapping economic crises, many countries face renewed pressure to devalue their currencies. Yet, despite extensive research, the effects of devaluation on national income remain insufficiently understood. This study examines the income effects of the 1994 CFA franc devaluation on Franc Zone economies using two new indicators—Revealed Comparative Income (RCI) and Revealed Comparative Export (RCX)—which measure a country’s relative position in global income and export hierarchies. We find that for most Franc Zone countries, both RCI and RCX declined in the short and long term. The only exception is Equatorial Guinea, a small country with fewer than two million people, whose position improved due to oil discovery and exploitation. The short-term declines in RCI and RCX inevitably lead to reductions in nominal GDP right after devaluation. Combined with production expansion, this implies greater resource use alongside middle-class contraction. More fundamentally, devaluation often weakens a country’s capacity to generate income internationally, making it stuck in a lower position in the global hierarchy. Therefore, extreme caution is warranted when considering devaluation policies for developing economies.

abstract: This paper studies how residence rights shape the native-welfare effects of foreign-worker admissions when native and foreign labor are imperfect substitutes and foreign-background children require compensatory public-school resources. We develop an overlapping-generations general-equilibrium model comparing a restricted-residence regime, in which foreign workers work in the host country but conduct childrearing and retirement abroad, with an open-residence regime, in which foreign workers may settle with their families. Under restricted residence, higher admissions can raise native steady-state welfare when native and foreign labor are sufficiently weak substitutes, even if native wages fall, because the education channel is absent and general-equilibrium adjustments through capital accumulation and the interest rate may offset wage losses. Under open residence, family settlement activates an education-resource burden. The marginal welfare effect of admissions decomposes into a non-education component and an education-resource component, yielding a closed-form threshold for the relative public-school resource requirement. Under open residence, a marginal increase in foreign-worker admissions raises native welfare when the non-education gains are sufficiently large relative to the compensatory education-resource burden. The results show that the welfare effect of foreign-worker admissions depends jointly on labor-market substitutability, residence rights, and the public-school resources required to educate foreign-background children in the host country.
title: Residence rights and native welfare: the education channel under imperfect substitutability

abstract: This paper examines the effect of Italy’s Law 215/2012, which introduced gender-balanced double-preference voting in municipal councils, on attacks against local politicians. Using a staggered difference-in-differences design focusing on municipalities with 5000–15,000 inhabitants, we find that the reform increases both the probability and the number of attacks in high-incidence regions—namely Apulia, Calabria, and Campania. We provide suggestive evidence on the underlying mechanisms. In these regions, the reform increases women’s representation in municipal councils and is associated with higher educational attainment among politicians, including mayors and aldermen, who are more exposed to violence. These changes appear to make political bodies less permeable to external pressure aimed at extracting private benefits. Consistent with this interpretation, the reform leads to an increase in both attacks characterized by criminally coded intimidation and those with broader retaliatory features. However, we find no effect on indicators of corruption risk in public procurement, suggesting that the phenomenon is unlikely to be driven by large-scale corruption
journal: Journal of Economic Behavior and Organization
source_issue: Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization, Volume 252
title: Gender quotas, political selection, and violence. Evidence from high-incidence areas in Italy

abstract: In most Global South cities, peri-urban land operates like the new gold. The peri-urban frontier has increasingly become a site of intense land commodification, as financialization transforms land from a source of agro-based livelihoods into a speculative asset devoid of any collective or social significance. This paper adds to the emerging work on the uneven geographies of speculative land transformations by examining how the financialization of peri-urban land generates a crisis of social reproduction, undermining households’ capacity to secure livelihoods, housing, and food. Drawing on a qualitative case study approach and in-depth interviews with peri-urban residents and key-informants in the Agona West Municipality, the study findings highlight the systemic exclusion of women from peri-urban land transactions, intensification of gender inequalities in accessing productive resources, and the erosion of social care and support systems. The findings further reveal the rapid transformation of traditional livelihood systems from predominantly agrarian to informal and precarious urban labour. The paper fronts the need for urban development and land management frameworks that safeguard livelihoods, promote equitable land use, and reconcile development with social justice. By foregrounding the intersection of land financialization and social reproduction systems, the paper contributes to emerging discourses on just urban transitions in the often-overlooked smaller and intermediate towns of the Global South.
title: On the land rush in the peri-urban frontier: Land financialization and the crisis of social reproduction in Ghana

abstract: We examine how negative environmental and social (E&S) incidents affect consumer behavior and firms’ responses. Using high-frequency store-visit data from SafeGraph linked to firm E&S incidents from RepRisk, we find that negative incidents lead to a modest decline in store visits on average, with substantially larger reductions among more environmentally and socially conscious consumers in Democratic-leaning areas. The effects are stronger for more severe and influential incidents, among younger and more educated consumers, for firms with higher pre-incident advertising intensity and E&S ratings, and in more competitive markets. Following these incidents, firms temporarily reduce discretionary disclosures and increase advertising expenditures over the longer run. Together, the results highlight consumer behavior as a way in which E&S incidents affect firm cash flows and suggest that firms adjust disclosure and advertising following these incidents.
title: From incidents to outcomes: consumer reactions and firm responses to negative environmental and social practices

abstract: The market for rare earth elements is relatively small in value, but shortages can lead to disproportionate output losses. This column introduces a network model to quantify the output losses from a large and permanent shortage of rare earth elements. At short horizons less than one year, GDP losses range from 0.6% in the UK to 1.5% in the US and 1.8% in Japan. Supply chain risk assessments need to incorporate production networks to understand the vulnerabilities from such disruptions. Policymakers should build strategic reserves and develop domestic capacity to help withstand the short-run losses from rare earth shortages.
authors: Christian Bogmans, Maximiliano Jerez Osses, Jorge Miranda-Pinto, Jean-Marc Natal

abstract: Temporary fuel-tax cuts are eventually restored, making both policy directions relevant for consumer incidence. Using ordinary and tax-exempt prices for the same gasoline and diesel in Korea, we compare two cuts and two restorations in 2018–2021. Over days 1–7 after each reform, full-sample, equal-event pass-through averages about 70% for cuts and 54–55% for restorations. Same-station comparisons and checks for sample composition, cost adjustment, and local shocks retain this point ordering. Pretrend and no-reform diagnostics nevertheless reveal differential price movements. Under stated restrictions, sensitivity bounds limit the size of a firm-favorable restoration-minus-cut gap, although the negative sign is less robust to departures from parallel trends. The results document incomplete initial consumer relief and lower estimated first-week pass-through when relief is withdrawn, with diagnostics quantifying the implications of differential price adjustment.
title: Does what goes up come back down? Pass-through of fuel-tax cuts and restorations in Korea

abstract: The EU's decision to phase out Russian natural gas imports raises concerns about the economic consequences of the ban, particularly its timing and uneven regional impacts. This paper examines how the wholesale gas price effects of eliminating Russian supplies depend on changing market conditions, including global LNG availability, infrastructure development and European gas demand. Using a European gas market model, we compare the impacts of an immediate phase-out under 2024 market conditions with those of a gradual phase-out under projected 2028 conditions, while distinguishing the effects of the ban from broader market developments. The results show that an immediate phase-out would lead to significant regional price increase, particularly in Central and South-Eastern Europe (4-5 €/MWh), where infrastructure constraints limit access to alternative supplies. By contrast, under projected 2028 market conditions, the ban would increase average EU wholesale gas prices by only 0.3 €/MWh and gas procurement costs by approximately 1%. Extending the phase-out to neighbouring non-EU countries would increase costs, particularly in the Western Balkans. Global market circumstances have by magnitude greater impact on absolute price levels than the Russian gas phaseout itself. The findings suggest that a coordinated phase-out of Russian gas can be achieved with limited additional wholesale market costs, provided that sufficient alternative supplies and infrastructure are available. They also highlight the importance of regional cooperation and continued supply diversification to mitigate uneven impacts across European gas markets.
title: Can Europe afford to phase out Russian gas? How timing, global supply conditions, and demand shape wholesale gas prices

abstract: This paper revisits fiscal policy in a currency union using a behavioral New Keynesian model with cognitive discounting à la Gabaix (2020). Cognitive discounting reshapes the government spending multiplier through three channels: a non-Ricardian effect, as households underweight future taxes; an expectation-dampening effect, which weakens forward inflation transmission; and a TOT effect, which slows terms-of-trade adjustment. At the ZLB, the welfare gain from discretionary fiscal coordination is positive but small in the two-country model. Stronger cognitive discounting generally reduces this gain by weakening inflation expectation transmission. Moreover, the gains are asymmetric: the directly shocked country benefits more, while its partner also benefits over the empirically relevant calibration range of cognitive discounting.
title: Fiscal policy in a behavioral New Keynesian model for the currency union

abstract: Urban residents increasingly purchase or construct second homes in surrounding rural settlements for leisure and temporary stays, creating new forms of interaction between urban demand and rural land and livelihoods. Although second-home development is often regarded as an opportunity for rural revitalization and economic diversification, its actual contribution to host communities remains uncertain, particularly in areas where land-use governance and institutional capacity are limited. This study examines the socio-economic effects of second-home tourism on rural households in Ferdows County, eastern Iran, with a focus on livelihoods, land-use change, and relations between local residents and second-home owners. The study uses survey data collected from 320 rural households in 14 villages and applies quantitative and spatial analyses to assess economic and social outcomes. The results indicate that second-home tourism has generated only limited local development benefits. Economic outcomes, including employment generation, income diversification, and local investment, remain weak, while social outcomes are characterized by tensions between permanent residents and second-home owners, declining social cohesion, and unequal access to services. Significant differences among villages further reveal the uneven spatial distribution of these impacts. The findings further suggest that fragmented institutional coordination and limited community participation have constrained the potential benefits of second-home development. Overall, the study shows that urban demand for second homes does not necessarily translate into rural development. Its local consequences depend in important ways on how land-use is governed and how local communities are involved in planning and decision-making. An integrated policy framework is therefore required to regulate land-use, strengthen local governance, align second-home development with regional sustainability objectives, and ensure meaningful community participation in planning and decision-making.
title: Urban-driven second-home expansion and uneven transformation in peri-urban settlements: Socio-economic implications and planning challenges
